newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Police jeep firebombed in Taiwan nuclear protest.
newsitem.headline: Police jeep firebombed in Taiwan nuclear protest.

text.p: Anti-nuclear protesters stormed a police line and fire-bombed a police jeep near parliament on Friday as tempers flared hours before a crucial vote on the fate of Taiwan's fourth nuclear power station.
Activists hurled petrol bombs from a truck that crashed through a razor-wire barricade a few hundred metres from parliament and the presidential palace, setting a police jeep ablaze, police said.

Parts of Taipei's government district were sealed off to control a day of pro- and anti-nuclear protests as parliament debated whether to uphold its cancellation of the US$4.1 billion needed to complete the unfinished nuclear plant.

The cabinet had appealed against the cancellation, setting the stage for Friday's final vote. Opponents needed to muster a two-thirds vote to make the decision stand, no easy feat in view of the ruling Nationalist Party's 51 percent majority.

Opposition Democratic Progressive Party lawmakers, determined to prevent a vote they were unlikely to win, donned green headbands and launched a filibuster, occupying the parliament dais and vowing to stay on until midnight (1600 GMT).
"We will not give in," said Shen Fu-hsiung of the Democratic Progressive Party.
Fistfights and shoving erupted on Friday evening as parliament leaders sought to clear the dais and proceed with the vote.

Friday's protests were raucous but peaceful until the truck ploughed into the barricade and 20 to 30 activists swinging banners mounted on poles jumped out to clash with police armed with shields and clubs, police said.
At least two demonstrators were detained.
One police officer was hit by the truck and a reporter was roughed up, police said. Both had only minor injuries.
Parliament humiliated the Nationalist government in May by cancelling funding, but state utility Taiwan Power has pushed ahead pending the outcome of Friday's vote.
Hanging in the balance was U.S. giant General Electric's US$1.8 billion contract to supply the light-water plant's twin reactors and generators.
Turning to increasingly militant tactics, opposition lawmakers tried to kill the project on Tuesday by physically barring Premier Lien Chan from parliament to defend the cabinet's appeal.
Lien, who assailed the strongarm tactics as a "dark day for democracy", took the case for nuclear power directly to the public on Thursday with a live television appeal.
Taiwan Power already has sunk US$220 million into the 2,700-megawatt nuclear station outside Taipei.
